major_deficiencies.description: No major deficiencies identified by the regulatory reviewer. The totality-of-evidence framework — analytical similarity, three-way PK bridge (Study 20110216), and comparative clinical data (Study 20120265) — adequately supports biosimilarity. The margin discrepancy (sponsor's 0.67–1.50 vs. FDA's 0.73–1.36) and the use of EU-bevacizumab as the clinical comparator were acknowledged limitations but are not blocking given the observed 90% CI (0.80–1.09) falling within the stricter FDA margin and the well-established analytical/PK bridge. Extrapolation to non-studied indications is scientifically justified under the 351(k) framework. No regulatory major deficiency.

No major deficiencies identified by the clinical reviewer. The primary endpoint (ORR RR 0.93, 90% CI 0.80–1.09) meets both the sponsor's and FDA's equivalence margins. The numerically shorter PFS in the ABP215 arm (6.6 vs. 7.9 months, HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.80–1.34) is directionally noted but the wide CI, limited event maturity, and exploratory-only role of PFS in a biosimilarity exercise preclude it from constituting a major deficiency. EGFR/ALK mutation status incompleteness is a reviewable issue addressable through labeling and sensitivity analyses, not a blocking deficiency. No clinical major deficiency.

No major deficiencies identified by the toxicology reviewer. The nonclinical comparability package (xenograft models, VEGF permeability assay, rat PK, 1-month cynomolgus monkey repeat-dose study) revealed no biologically significant differences between ABP215 and US-licensed Avastin. Structural attribute differences (high mannose glycans, galactosylation, charge variants, FcγRIIIa 158V binding) were each characterized and mitigated through functional assays and clinical PK data. The small group size in the monkey study (n=3/sex/group) is a limitation consistent with ICH S9 and the biosimilar framework. No toxicology major deficiency.

No major deficiencies identified by the clinical pharmacology reviewer. Three-way PK equivalence was rigorously demonstrated in Study 20110216 (all pairwise 90% CIs for AUCinf, AUClast, and Cmax within 80–125%). The higher high-mannose glycan content in bevacizumab-awwb — the most substantive analytical difference with theoretical PK implications — is adequately mitigated by the AUCinf 90% CI (94.0–102.9%) and comparable trough concentrations in Study 265. Restriction of Study 20110216 to healthy males is a design limitation pre-agreed with FDA and bridged by Study 265 trough data. Absence of a formal popPK/E-R analysis is not required under 351(k) when PK similarity is established via the standard bioequivalence framework. A PMC for glycan mapping method validation appropriately addresses residual uncertainty. No clinical pharmacology major deficiency.

No major deficiencies identified by the biostatistics reviewer. The primary statistical framework (TOST equivalence, 90% CI, ITT, stratified GLM with log link, pre-specified margins) is appropriate and rigorously executed. The margin discrepancy is resolved in practice by the observed CI (0.80–1.09) clearing the stricter FDA margin (0.73–1.36). Sample size adequacy under FDA's tighter margin (~80% power) is a theoretical concern rendered moot by the realized ORR and tight CI. PFS imbalance (6.6 vs. 7.9 months) is consistent with no meaningful difference given the wide CI and limited event maturity. EGFR/ALK data incompleteness does not materially threaten the primary ORR comparison given low prevalence and balanced distribution. No biostatistics major deficiency.

No major deficiencies identified by the CMC reviewer. The analytical similarity package (19 ABP215 lots, 27 US-Avastin lots, 29 EU-bevacizumab lots) is extensive and covers all critical quality attributes. Identified attribute differences (elevated high mannose glycans with an increasing lot-to-lot trend, charge variant differences, FcγRIIIa 158V binding difference, low endotoxin recovery in the detection method, DS long-term stability acceptance criteria pending ≥5-lot data, and HCP method validation) are each characterized, mitigated through orthogonal data and functional assays, and appropriately deferred as post-marketing commitments (PMCs). None individually or collectively rises to the level of a blocking deficiency. The use of the VEGFA111 isoform in the HUVEC potency assay is a non-standard substrate but acceptability is confirmed through orthogonal data. No CMC major deficiency.

blind_positions.summary: BLA 761028 for MVASI (bevacizumab-awwb) is a 351(k) biosimilar application referencing US-licensed Avastin (bevacizumab). From a regulatory/clinical perspective, the totality of evidence — extensive analytical similarity data, a three-way PK similarity study in healthy volunteers (Study 20110216), and a randomized double-blind comparative clinical study in NSCLC (Study 20120265) — adequately supports a demonstration of no clinically meaningful differences between ABP215 and US-licensed Avastin. The primary endpoint (ORR risk ratio 0.93, 90% CI 0.80–1.09) fell within both the sponsor's pre-specified margin (0.67, 1.50) and FDA's recommended margin (0.73, 1.36). The scientific bridge between EU-approved bevacizumab, US-licensed Avastin, and ABP215 is adequately established analytically and pharmacokinetically. Extrapolation to non-studied indications is scientifically justified based on shared mechanism of action (VEGF inhibition), consistent PK, and comparable safety profile. No new safety signals were identified. The application is approvable from a regulatory standpoint, with minor reviewable issues addressable through labeling and post-marketing commitments.
key_concerns: Sponsor's pre-specified equivalence margin (0.67, 1.50) was wider than FDA's recommended margin (0.73, 1.36); however, the 90% CI (0.80, 1.09) fell within both margins, rendering this a non-issue for the final determination.

Study 265 used EU-approved bevacizumab as the comparator rather than US-licensed Avastin; adequacy of the scientific bridge (analytical + PK) is critical — the bridge is well-established and FDA agreed to this design.

Sample size was powered for the sponsor's wider margin (0.67, 1.50) rather than FDA's recommended margin (0.73, 1.36); FDA acknowledged this limitation in January 2015 and agreed to evaluate in the context of totality of evidence — the observed CI is well within FDA's margin, mitigating this concern.

Extrapolation to five non-studied indications (mCRC, GBM, mRCC, cervical cancer) relies on shared MOA, PK similarity, and safety comparability rather than direct clinical data in each indication; this is consistent with 351(k) biosimilar extrapolation framework under FDA guidance.
Orphan exclusivity for ovarian cancer indications appropriately excluded from the application — no regulatory deficiency.

Immunogenicity rates were low and comparable (ABP215: 1.4% treatment-induced ADA; EU-bevacizumab: 2.5%); no neutralizing ADA assessment was deemed necessary by FDA, consistent with the known low immunogenicity profile of bevacizumab.

EGFR/ALK mutation status was not systematically assessed in Study 265 (>55% 'not performed' for EGFR); FDA had previously requested sensitivity analyses for EGFR wild-type/ALK-negative subpopulations — this is a reviewable issue given that the ORR in the ITT population (including potential EGFR-mutant patients who would not receive bevacizumab in standard practice) is the primary comparator, but the observed ORR in the bevacizumab arm (41.7%) is consistent with historical data for the intended population.

Slightly higher SAE rate in ABP215 arm (26%) vs. bevacizumab arm (23%) and slightly higher Grade 3-4 hemorrhagic events (2% vs. 1%) warrant labeling attention but are not clinically meaningful differences and are within expected bevacizumab class-effect ranges.

deficiencies.description: Sponsor's pre-specified similarity margin (0.67, 1.50) was wider than FDA's recommended margin (0.73, 1.36), and the study was powered for the sponsor's margin rather than FDA's. This represents a protocol design deviation from FDA's December 2014 advice letter. However, because the observed 90% CI (0.80, 1.09) falls comfortably within FDA's more stringent margin of (0.73, 1.36), the underlying evidentiary standard is met and this does not constitute a blocking deficiency. FDA acknowledged the logistical constraints in January 2015 and committed to evaluating in the totality-of-evidence context.

EGFR and ALK mutation status was not performed in the majority of Study 265 patients (>55% EGFR 'not performed'; >74% ALK 'not done'). FDA had specifically requested sensitivity analyses for EGFR wild-type/ALK-negative subpopulations to ensure the comparator population reflects the intended bevacizumab-eligible population. The absence of complete molecular profiling introduces uncertainty about whether the ITT ORR comparison is fully representative of the labeled population. This is addressable through labeling context and does not alter the biosimilarity conclusion, as the observed ORR in the bevacizumab arm (41.7%) is consistent with historical bevacizumab data in non-squamous NSCLC and the risk ratio is robust across sensitivity analyses.

blind_positions.summary: BLA 761028 seeks licensure of ABP215 (bevacizumab-awwb, MVASI) as a biosimilar to US-licensed Avastin (bevacizumab) across all non-orphan-protected indications. The pivotal comparative clinical study (Study 20120265) was conducted in first-line non-squamous NSCLC patients receiving carboplatin/paclitaxel backbone, comparing ABP215 to EU-approved bevacizumab. The primary endpoint — risk ratio of ORR by independent radiologic review — was 0.93 (90% CI: 0.80–1.09), falling within both the applicant's pre-specified margin (0.67, 1.50) and FDA's recommended margin (0.73, 1.36). Secondary endpoints (DoR, PFS) and safety/immunogenicity data were comparable between arms. A robust analytical similarity package, a validated PK bridge (Study 20110216) establishing three-way PK equivalence among ABP215, US-licensed Avastin, and EU-approved bevacizumab, and a scientifically justified extrapolation framework collectively support the totality-of-evidence biosimilarity determination. No new safety signals were identified. From a clinical/medical oncology standpoint, the application meets the biosimilarity standard and supports approval across the sought indications.
key_concerns: The primary equivalence margin used by the sponsor (0.67, 1.50) was wider than FDA's recommended margin (0.73, 1.36); however, the observed 90% CI (0.80, 1.09) falls comfortably within the FDA-recommended margin, rendering this a non-issue for the final determination.

Study 20120265 used EU-approved bevacizumab rather than US-licensed Avastin as the direct comparator; the scientific bridge (analytical + PK) adequately justifies reliance on these data, but the indirect nature of the comparison is an inherent limitation of the biosimilar development program.

Extrapolation to non-studied indications (mCRC, GBM, mRCC, cervical cancer) relies on shared VEGF-inhibition mechanism of action, PK similarity, and comparable toxicity profiles rather than direct clinical data in each indication; this is scientifically justified per 351(k) biosimilar framework but warrants acknowledgment.

PFS numerically favored the EU-bevacizumab arm (7.9 vs. 6.6 months, HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.80–1.34); while the HR is consistent with no meaningful difference and the CI is wide, this directional imbalance should be noted in labeling context, though it does not undermine the biosimilarity conclusion.

A small proportion of patients had EGFR-positive or ALK-positive tumors (2.1% and 1.2% in ABP215 arm, respectively); these patients would not typically receive bevacizumab-based therapy in current practice, but their inclusion does not materially affect the biosimilarity assessment given the small numbers and balanced distribution.

Immunogenicity rates were low and comparable (treatment-induced ADA: 1.4% ABP215 vs. 2.5% EU-bevacizumab), with no apparent PK, efficacy, or safety impact; this is reassuring but the slightly higher numerically observed ADA rate in the reference arm should be monitored post-approval.

The safety profile in Study 265 — including VEGF-class toxicities (hypertension 19% vs. 16%, hemorrhage 22% vs. 21%, Grade 3-4 events 42% vs. 44%) — is consistent with the well-characterized bevacizumab safety profile; no new signals identified.

blind_positions.summary: ABP215 (bevacizumab-awwb, MVASI) is a proposed biosimilar to US-licensed Avastin submitted under the 351(k) pathway. From a nonclinical/toxicology perspective, the submission is well-structured and adequate. The applicant provided a comprehensive nonclinical comparability package including in vivo xenograft tumor models (A431 epidermoid and Colo205 colorectal), a VEGF-induced vascular permeability assay, a single-dose rat PK study, and a 1-month repeat-dose toxicology study in cynomolgus monkeys. No biologically significant differences in pharmacology, pharmacokinetics, or toxicity were identified between ABP215 and US-licensed Avastin (bevacizumab) across these studies. The nonclinical data, in the context of the well-characterized safety profile of the reference product bevacizumab, support the conclusion that ABP215 poses no new or unexpected nonclinical safety risks. The dose used in the clinical program (15 mg/kg IV q3w for NSCLC) is consistent with the approved reference product dose and is supported by the established bevacizumab clinical pharmacology and safety database. No blocking nonclinical deficiencies are identified.
key_concerns: Project Optimus dose justification: The proposed dose (15 mg/kg q3w for NSCLC; 10 mg/kg q2w for other indications) mirrors the reference product's approved doses and was not independently optimized for ABP215. However, given the biosimilar regulatory framework under 351(k), dose optimization is inherited from the reference product's established clinical program and is not a new requirement for the biosimilar applicant.

High mannose glycan content: Bevacizumab-awwb contains higher levels of high mannose N-linked glycans compared to US-licensed Avastin and EU-approved bevacizumab. Higher high mannose content can theoretically accelerate clearance via mannose receptor-mediated pathways, potentially affecting PK and thereby the exposure-toxicity relationship. This was mitigated by PK similarity data in Study 20110216 and trough concentration comparability in Study 20120265, and a PMC for glycan mapping method validation was included.

Galactosylation differences: Bevacizumab-awwb showed differences in galactosylated N-linked glycans relative to the reference product. Galactose levels can influence CDC activity. This was addressed by C1q binding studies and CDC activity assays in multiple cell lines, all of which showed no meaningful differences in effector function.

FcγRIIIa (158V) binding difference: A noted difference in binding to the 158V isotype of FcγRIIIa was identified. Given that bevacizumab targets a soluble ligand (VEGFA) and ADCC is not part of its mechanism of action, and given that ADCC activity assays in relevant cell lines showed no meaningful differences, this is not considered a safety concern.

Charge variant differences: Higher levels of C-terminal lysine and other basic/acidic charge variants were observed in bevacizumab-awwb. Characterization data demonstrated that the same types of variants are present in all three products, and in vitro potency was not meaningfully impacted even at dramatically elevated levels. C-terminal lysine is rapidly removed in vivo.

Reproductive and developmental toxicity: No new reproductive/developmental toxicity studies were conducted for ABP215. This is appropriate under ICH S9 for anticancer biologics and the 351(k) biosimilar framework; the reference product's established reproductive risk profile (fetal harm, ovarian failure) is carried forward into labeling.

1-month monkey toxicology study: The repeat-dose toxicology study was limited to 1 month in cynomolgus monkeys (n=3/sex/group). While this is consistent with ICH S9 guidance for anticancer biologics and the biosimilar comparability framework, the small group size limits statistical power for detecting subtle toxicological differences. No biologically significant differences were observed.
Genotoxicity: No genotoxicity studies were submitted, which is appropriate per ICH S9 for a recombinant monoclonal antibody anticancer biologic.

deficiencies.description: High mannose glycan content in bevacizumab-awwb is higher than in US-licensed Avastin and EU-approved bevacizumab. While this was adequately mitigated by PK similarity data and a PMC for glycan mapping method validation, the ongoing monitoring of this attribute is important to ensure no future PK drift that could alter the exposure-toxicity relationship. This is addressable as a post-marketing commitment and does not constitute a blocking deficiency.

blind_positions.summary: ABP215 (bevacizumab-awwb, MVASI) is a proposed biosimilar to US-licensed Avastin submitted under Section 351(k). From a clinical pharmacology perspective, the application is well-supported. PK similarity between ABP215 and US-licensed Avastin was rigorously demonstrated in Study 20110216, a 3-arm parallel-group single-dose study in 202 healthy male subjects, with all three pairwise 90% CIs for AUCinf, AUClast, and Cmax falling within the pre-specified 80–125% bounds. The scientific PK bridge between ABP215, US-licensed Avastin, and EU-approved bevacizumab is adequately established, justifying reliance on Study 265 data. Immunogenicity rates were low and comparable across arms, with no apparent PK, efficacy, or safety impact from ADA. Trough concentrations in Study 265 were comparable between arms, providing supportive multiple-dose PK data in the target patient population. One minor analytical concern regarding higher high-mannose glycan content in bevacizumab-awwb was adequately mitigated by PK and clinical data, with a PMC for glycan mapping method validation appropriately assigned. No clinically meaningful PK differences were identified that would preclude approval.
key_concerns: Higher high-mannose glycan content in bevacizumab-awwb vs. US-licensed Avastin and EU-approved bevacizumab: high mannose can accelerate clearance via mannose receptor-mediated uptake, potentially reducing AUC and Cmin. However, the 90% CI for AUCinf in Study 20110216 (94.0–102.9%) and comparable trough concentrations in Study 265 confirm no clinically meaningful PK impact at the levels observed.

PK similarity study (Study 20110216) was conducted exclusively in healthy male subjects. Bevacizumab clearance is known to differ by sex; however, the study design was pre-agreed with FDA and the restriction to males was specifically intended to reduce inter-subject PK variability. Trough data from Study 265 (mixed-sex NSCLC patients) provide supportive bridging evidence.

Immunogenicity sampling in Study 20110216 was limited to pre-dose Day 1 and post-dose Day 84 only, which may not capture early transient ADA. However, Study 265 provided more granular longitudinal ADA sampling (Weeks 1, 4, 7, 13, and end of study), and overall ADA incidence was low (1.4% ABP215 vs. 2.5% EU-bevacizumab) with no PK or safety impact.

No formal population PK (popPK) model or exposure-response (E-R) analysis was submitted. For a biosimilar application under 351(k), this is not a regulatory requirement when PK similarity is demonstrated via the standard bioequivalence framework; the dose is inherited from the reference product with an established E-R relationship.

Neutralizing ADA assessment was waived by FDA based on the low incidence of binding ADA, the nature of the soluble VEGF target, and publicly available bevacizumab immunogenicity data. This is acceptable and consistent with FDA's risk-based immunogenicity framework.

blind_positions.summary: Study 20120265 (Study 265) is a randomized, double-blind, parallel-group Phase 3 equivalence trial comparing ABP-215 to EU-approved bevacizumab in 642 patients with advanced non-squamous NSCLC. The primary endpoint — risk ratio (RR) of ORR assessed by central independent radiologists — yielded RR = 0.93 (90% CI: 0.80, 1.09), which falls entirely within both the applicant's pre-specified margin (0.67, 1.50) and FDA's recommended tighter margin (0.73, 1.36). Secondary endpoints (DoR: 5.8 vs. 5.6 months; PFS HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.80–1.34) are directionally consistent and do not suggest meaningful inferiority. The margin derivation is grounded in a pre-specified meta-analysis of four historical NSCLC trials (N=1,675), and the observed ORR in the EU-bevacizumab arm (41.7%) is consistent with the meta-analytic estimate (37.7%), validating the historical control assumption. The statistical framework is appropriate for a biosimilarity exercise: a two-one-sided test (TOST) equivalence approach with 90% CI, ITT primary analysis, stratified GLM with log link, and pre-specified margins. No interim efficacy analyses were conducted, preserving the full alpha. Randomization was stratified by region, ECOG PS, and sex, and baseline characteristics are well-balanced. The one notable statistical tension — FDA's preferred margin of (0.73, 1.36) vs. the applicant's wider margin of (0.67, 1.50) — is resolved in practice because the observed 90% CI (0.80, 1.09) comfortably clears the stricter FDA margin, making the margin disagreement moot. From a biostatistics perspective, the primary evidence is robust and the application is approvable.
key_concerns: Margin discrepancy: applicant pre-specified (0.67, 1.50) vs. FDA-recommended (0.73, 1.36). Study was fully enrolled before FDA issued its December 2014 advice letter, so the wider margin was locked in. However, the observed 90% CI (0.80, 1.09) clears even the stricter FDA margin, rendering this a non-issue for the final determination.

Sample size was powered (>95%) for the applicant's wider margin (0.67, 1.50) at the assumed ORR of ~38%. Under FDA's tighter margin (0.73, 1.36), the enrolled N=642 provides approximately 80% power — adequate but not as comfortable. The realized ORR (~40%) and tight CI make this a theoretical rather than practical concern.

PFS as a secondary endpoint shows median 6.6 vs. 7.9 months (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.80–1.34). The wide CI and the 1.3-month median difference are consistent with no meaningful difference but reflect limited PFS follow-up and event maturity (40% events in each arm); this is acceptable for a biosimilarity exercise where PFS is exploratory/supportive only.

Subgroup analyses of ORR by gender, age, race, and region are presented but are exploratory and not multiplicity-controlled. No subgroup shows a directionally concerning signal that would undermine the primary conclusion.

EGFR/ALK mutation status was not systematically collected (>55% 'not performed' in both arms). FDA had flagged this at the July 2013 meeting. The applicant provided sensitivity analyses; given the low prevalence of actionable mutations in the enrolled population and the balanced distribution of known mutation status across arms, this does not materially threaten the primary ORR comparison.

The ITT population is the pre-specified primary analysis population, which is appropriate. The treated population (safety) is nearly identical (98.8% and 98.4% treated), minimizing any ITT vs. per-protocol divergence concern.
Censoring rules for PFS and DoR are standard RECIST-based; no evidence of informative censoring or differential dropout patterns that would bias the secondary endpoints.

deficiencies.description: Margin discrepancy between applicant's pre-specified equivalence margin (0.67, 1.50) and FDA's recommended margin (0.73, 1.36). The study was powered and designed to the wider margin. However, because the observed 90% CI (0.80, 1.09) falls entirely within the stricter FDA margin, this discrepancy has no practical consequence for the approvability determination. This is a non-blocking, documentation-level issue.

blind_positions.summary: BLA 761028 for MVASI (bevacizumab-awwb) presents a comprehensive CMC package supporting biosimilarity to US-licensed Avastin. The analytical similarity assessment using 19 bevacizumab-awwb lots, 27 US-licensed Avastin lots, and 29 EU-approved bevacizumab lots is extensive and covers primary structure, higher-order structure, biological activity (Fab- and Fc-mediated), product-related impurities, and process-related impurities. Several attribute differences were identified (high mannose glycans, galactosylation, charge variants, FcγRIIIa 158V binding, aggregates/fragments), but each was adequately characterized and mitigated through orthogonal data, functional assays, and/or clinical PK confirmation. The manufacturing process at Amgen Thousand Oaks (DS) and the designated DP fill site is described as well-controlled and validated. Drug product stability is supported for a 36-month shelf life at 2–8°C. Four post-marketing commitments (PMCs) address residual uncertainties in DS stability acceptance criteria, glycan mapping method validation, HCP detection method validation, and endotoxin detection. None of these residual issues rise to the level of a blocking deficiency; each is appropriately deferred as a PMC. The scientific bridge between bevacizumab-awwb, US-licensed Avastin, and EU-approved bevacizumab is analytically and pharmacokinetically supported. From a CMC perspective, the application meets the standard for approval.
key_concerns: Elevated high mannose glycan content in bevacizumab-awwb relative to US-licensed Avastin and EU-approved bevacizumab, with a noted increasing trend over time in bevacizumab-awwb lots — potential PK impact mitigated by clinical PK data and manufacturing controls, but warrants ongoing monitoring via PMC for glycan mapping method validation.

Differences in charge variant profiles (higher HC C-terminal lysine, differences in acidic and basic peak fractions) — characterized and assessed as clinically inactive based on in vitro potency data and clinical PK; not blocking but requires continued control strategy oversight.
Differences in FcγRIIIa (158V) binding — mitigated by lack of ADCC activity in functional assays and the predominantly soluble VEGFA target MOA; not blocking.

Low endotoxin recovery (LER) issue in the endotoxin detection method — addressed through pyrogen testing at release and a PMC to develop a validated LER-resistant assay; not blocking but must be tracked.
DS stability acceptance criteria for the long-term storage condition require re-evaluation once data from ≥5 lots are available — deferred as PMC; not blocking.

Use of VEGFA111 isoform (not naturally expressed in human tissue or tumors) in the HUVEC proliferation potency assay — acceptability confirmed through orthogonal binding and degradation sensitivity data, but represents a non-standard assay substrate that should be monitored.
HCP detection method validation (including LC-MS and 2D-DIGE) deferred as PMC — not blocking given existing ELISA data and process controls.

deficiencies.description: Elevated and time-trending high mannose glycan content in bevacizumab-awwb lots relative to US-licensed Avastin and EU-approved bevacizumab. Higher high mannose levels can accelerate in vivo clearance via mannose receptor-mediated uptake, potentially affecting PK and efficacy. An increasing trend across bevacizumab-awwb lots was observed. While clinical PK data (Study 20110216 and trough concentrations in Study 20120265) did not demonstrate a PK impact, the glycan mapping method used in the control strategy has not yet been fully validated, and the manufacturing control to cap high mannose content is not yet fully characterized. This is addressable via PMC (glycan mapping method validation and DS stability re-evaluation) and ongoing manufacturing controls, and does not rise to a blocking deficiency given the clinical PK data mitigation.

Low endotoxin recovery (LER) phenomenon identified in the endotoxin detection method used for drug product release. The current approach relies on pyrogen testing as a bridging control at release, which is less specific than a validated LAL method not subject to LER. A PMC has been issued to develop and implement a validated endotoxin detection method not subject to LER. This is a known industry issue with certain formulations and is appropriately managed as a PMC; it does not independently warrant a CRL.

Glycan mapping and HCP detection methods (LC-MS, 2D-DIGE) included in the control strategy have not yet been fully validated at the time of BLA submission. These are deferred as post-marketing commitments. Existing ELISA-based HCP data and the analytical similarity dataset provide adequate assurance for approval, but full method validation is required post-approval to ensure long-term control strategy robustness.

This is addressable through labeling context and does not alter the biosimilarity conclusion, as the observed ORR in the bevacizumab arm (41.7%) is consistent with historical bevacizumab data in non-squamous NSCLC and the risk ratio is robust across sensitivity analyses.

final_positions.summary: BLA 761028 seeks licensure of ABP215 (bevacizumab-awwb, MVASI) as a biosimilar to US-licensed Avastin (bevacizumab) across all non-orphan-protected indications. The pivotal comparative clinical study (Study 20120265) was conducted in first-line non-squamous NSCLC patients receiving carboplatin/paclitaxel backbone, comparing ABP215 to EU-approved bevacizumab. The primary endpoint — risk ratio of ORR by independent radiologic review — was 0.93 (90% CI: 0.80–1.09), falling within both the applicant's pre-specified margin (0.67, 1.50) and FDA's recommended margin (0.73, 1.36). Secondary endpoints (DoR, PFS) and safety/immunogenicity data were comparable between arms. A robust analytical similarity package, a validated PK bridge (Study 20110216) establishing three-way PK equivalence among ABP215, US-licensed Avastin, and EU-approved bevacizumab, and a scientifically justified extrapolation framework collectively support the totality-of-evidence biosimilarity determination. No new safety signals were identified. From a clinical/medical oncology standpoint, the application meets the biosimilarity standard and supports approval across the sought indications.
key_concerns: The primary equivalence margin used by the sponsor (0.67, 1.50) was wider than FDA's recommended margin (0.73, 1.36); however, the observed 90% CI (0.80, 1.09) falls comfortably within the FDA-recommended margin, rendering this a non-issue for the final determination.

Study 20120265 used EU-approved bevacizumab rather than US-licensed Avastin as the direct comparator; the scientific bridge (analytical + PK) adequately justifies reliance on these data, but the indirect nature of the comparison is an inherent limitation of the biosimilar development program.

Extrapolation to non-studied indications (mCRC, GBM, mRCC, cervical cancer) relies on shared VEGF-inhibition mechanism of action, PK similarity, and comparable toxicity profiles rather than direct clinical data in each indication; this is scientifically justified per 351(k) biosimilar framework but warrants acknowledgment.

PFS numerically favored the EU-bevacizumab arm (7.9 vs. 6.6 months, HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.80–1.34); while the HR is consistent with no meaningful difference and the CI is wide, this directional imbalance should be noted in labeling context, though it does not undermine the biosimilarity conclusion.

A small proportion of patients had EGFR-positive or ALK-positive tumors (2.1% and 1.2% in ABP215 arm, respectively); these patients would not typically receive bevacizumab-based therapy in current practice, but their inclusion does not materially affect the biosimilarity assessment given the small numbers and balanced distribution.

Immunogenicity rates were low and comparable (treatment-induced ADA: 1.4% ABP215 vs. 2.5% EU-bevacizumab), with no apparent PK, efficacy, or safety impact; this is reassuring but the slightly higher numerically observed ADA rate in the reference arm should be monitored post-approval.

The safety profile in Study 265 — including VEGF-class toxicities (hypertension 19% vs. 16%, hemorrhage 22% vs. 21%, Grade 3-4 events 42% vs. 44%) — is consistent with the well-characterized bevacizumab safety profile; no new signals identified.

final_positions.summary: ABP215 (bevacizumab-awwb, MVASI) is a proposed biosimilar to US-licensed Avastin submitted under the 351(k) pathway. From a nonclinical/toxicology perspective, the submission is well-structured and adequate. The applicant provided a comprehensive nonclinical comparability package including in vivo xenograft tumor models (A431 epidermoid and Colo205 colorectal), a VEGF-induced vascular permeability assay, a single-dose rat PK study, and a 1-month repeat-dose toxicology study in cynomolgus monkeys. No biologically significant differences in pharmacology, pharmacokinetics, or toxicity were identified between ABP215 and US-licensed Avastin (bevacizumab) across these studies. The nonclinical data, in the context of the well-characterized safety profile of the reference product bevacizumab, support the conclusion that ABP215 poses no new or unexpected nonclinical safety risks. The dose used in the clinical program (15 mg/kg IV q3w for NSCLC) is consistent with the approved reference product dose and is supported by the established bevacizumab clinical pharmacology and safety database. No blocking nonclinical deficiencies are identified.
key_concerns: Project Optimus dose justification: The proposed dose (15 mg/kg q3w for NSCLC; 10 mg/kg q2w for other indications) mirrors the reference product's approved doses and was not independently optimized for ABP215. However, given the biosimilar regulatory framework under 351(k), dose optimization is inherited from the reference product's established clinical program and is not a new requirement for the biosimilar applicant.

High mannose glycan content: Bevacizumab-awwb contains higher levels of high mannose N-linked glycans compared to US-licensed Avastin and EU-approved bevacizumab. Higher high mannose content can theoretically accelerate clearance via mannose receptor-mediated pathways, potentially affecting PK and thereby the exposure-toxicity relationship. This was mitigated by PK similarity data in Study 20110216 and trough concentration comparability in Study 20120265, and a PMC for glycan mapping method validation was included.

Galactosylation differences: Bevacizumab-awwb showed differences in galactosylated N-linked glycans relative to the reference product. Galactose levels can influence CDC activity. This was addressed by C1q binding studies and CDC activity assays in multiple cell lines, all of which showed no meaningful differences in effector function.

FcγRIIIa (158V) binding difference: A noted difference in binding to the 158V isotype of FcγRIIIa was identified. Given that bevacizumab targets a soluble ligand (VEGFA) and ADCC is not part of its mechanism of action, and given that ADCC activity assays in relevant cell lines showed no meaningful differences, this is not considered a safety concern.

Charge variant differences: Higher levels of C-terminal lysine and other basic/acidic charge variants were observed in bevacizumab-awwb. Characterization data demonstrated that the same types of variants are present in all three products, and in vitro potency was not meaningfully impacted even at dramatically elevated levels. C-terminal lysine is rapidly removed in vivo.

Reproductive and developmental toxicity: No new reproductive/developmental toxicity studies were conducted for ABP215. This is appropriate under ICH S9 for anticancer biologics and the 351(k) biosimilar framework; the reference product's established reproductive risk profile (fetal harm, ovarian failure) is carried forward into labeling.

1-month monkey toxicology study: The repeat-dose toxicology study was limited to 1 month in cynomolgus monkeys (n=3/sex/group). While this is consistent with ICH S9 guidance for anticancer biologics and the biosimilar comparability framework, the small group size limits statistical power for detecting subtle toxicological differences. No biologically significant differences were observed.
Genotoxicity: No genotoxicity studies were submitted, which is appropriate per ICH S9 for a recombinant monoclonal antibody anticancer biologic.

deficiencies.description: High mannose glycan content in bevacizumab-awwb is higher than in US-licensed Avastin and EU-approved bevacizumab. While this was adequately mitigated by PK similarity data and a PMC for glycan mapping method validation, the ongoing monitoring of this attribute is important to ensure no future PK drift that could alter the exposure-toxicity relationship. This is addressable as a post-marketing commitment and does not constitute a blocking deficiency.

final_positions.summary: ABP215 (bevacizumab-awwb, MVASI) is a proposed biosimilar to US-licensed Avastin submitted under Section 351(k). From a clinical pharmacology perspective, the application is well-supported. PK similarity between ABP215 and US-licensed Avastin was rigorously demonstrated in Study 20110216, a 3-arm parallel-group single-dose study in 202 healthy male subjects, with all three pairwise 90% CIs for AUCinf, AUClast, and Cmax falling within the pre-specified 80–125% bounds. The scientific PK bridge between ABP215, US-licensed Avastin, and EU-approved bevacizumab is adequately established, justifying reliance on Study 265 data. Immunogenicity rates were low and comparable across arms, with no apparent PK, efficacy, or safety impact from ADA. Trough concentrations in Study 265 were comparable between arms, providing supportive multiple-dose PK data in the target patient population. One minor analytical concern regarding higher high-mannose glycan content in bevacizumab-awwb was adequately mitigated by PK and clinical data, with a PMC for glycan mapping method validation appropriately assigned. No clinically meaningful PK differences were identified that would preclude approval.
key_concerns: Higher high-mannose glycan content in bevacizumab-awwb vs. US-licensed Avastin and EU-approved bevacizumab: high mannose can accelerate clearance via mannose receptor-mediated uptake, potentially reducing AUC and Cmin. However, the 90% CI for AUCinf in Study 20110216 (94.0–102.9%) and comparable trough concentrations in Study 265 confirm no clinically meaningful PK impact at the levels observed.

PK similarity study (Study 20110216) was conducted exclusively in healthy male subjects. Bevacizumab clearance is known to differ by sex; however, the study design was pre-agreed with FDA and the restriction to males was specifically intended to reduce inter-subject PK variability. Trough data from Study 265 (mixed-sex NSCLC patients) provide supportive bridging evidence.

Immunogenicity sampling in Study 20110216 was limited to pre-dose Day 1 and post-dose Day 84 only, which may not capture early transient ADA. However, Study 265 provided more granular longitudinal ADA sampling (Weeks 1, 4, 7, 13, and end of study), and overall ADA incidence was low (1.4% ABP215 vs. 2.5% EU-bevacizumab) with no PK or safety impact.

No formal population PK (popPK) model or exposure-response (E-R) analysis was submitted. For a biosimilar application under 351(k), this is not a regulatory requirement when PK similarity is demonstrated via the standard bioequivalence framework; the dose is inherited from the reference product with an established E-R relationship.

Neutralizing ADA assessment was waived by FDA based on the low incidence of binding ADA, the nature of the soluble VEGF target, and publicly available bevacizumab immunogenicity data. This is acceptable and consistent with FDA's risk-based immunogenicity framework.

final_positions.summary: Study 20120265 (Study 265) is a randomized, double-blind, parallel-group Phase 3 equivalence trial comparing ABP-215 to EU-approved bevacizumab in 642 patients with advanced non-squamous NSCLC. The primary endpoint — risk ratio (RR) of ORR assessed by central independent radiologists — yielded RR = 0.93 (90% CI: 0.80, 1.09), which falls entirely within both the applicant's pre-specified margin (0.67, 1.50) and FDA's recommended tighter margin (0.73, 1.36). Secondary endpoints (DoR: 5.8 vs. 5.6 months; PFS HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.80–1.34) are directionally consistent and do not suggest meaningful inferiority. The margin derivation is grounded in a pre-specified meta-analysis of four historical NSCLC trials (N=1,675), and the observed ORR in the EU-bevacizumab arm (41.7%) is consistent with the meta-analytic estimate (37.7%), validating the historical control assumption. The statistical framework is appropriate for a biosimilarity exercise: a two-one-sided test (TOST) equivalence approach with 90% CI, ITT primary analysis, stratified GLM with log link, and pre-specified margins. No interim efficacy analyses were conducted, preserving the full alpha. Randomization was stratified by region, ECOG PS, and sex, and baseline characteristics are well-balanced. The one notable statistical tension — FDA's preferred margin of (0.73, 1.36) vs. the applicant's wider margin of (0.67, 1.50) — is resolved in practice because the observed 90% CI (0.80, 1.09) comfortably clears the stricter FDA margin, making the margin disagreement moot. From a biostatistics perspective, the primary evidence is robust and the application is approvable.
key_concerns: Margin discrepancy: applicant pre-specified (0.67, 1.50) vs. FDA-recommended (0.73, 1.36). Study was fully enrolled before FDA issued its December 2014 advice letter, so the wider margin was locked in. However, the observed 90% CI (0.80, 1.09) clears even the stricter FDA margin, rendering this a non-issue for the final determination.

Sample size was powered (>95%) for the applicant's wider margin (0.67, 1.50) at the assumed ORR of ~38%. Under FDA's tighter margin (0.73, 1.36), the enrolled N=642 provides approximately 80% power — adequate but not as comfortable. The realized ORR (~40%) and tight CI make this a theoretical rather than practical concern.

PFS as a secondary endpoint shows median 6.6 vs. 7.9 months (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.80–1.34). The wide CI and the 1.3-month median difference are consistent with no meaningful difference but reflect limited PFS follow-up and event maturity (40% events in each arm); this is acceptable for a biosimilarity exercise where PFS is exploratory/supportive only.

Subgroup analyses of ORR by gender, age, race, and region are presented but are exploratory and not multiplicity-controlled. No subgroup shows a directionally concerning signal that would undermine the primary conclusion.

EGFR/ALK mutation status was not systematically collected (>55% 'not performed' in both arms). FDA had flagged this at the July 2013 meeting. The applicant provided sensitivity analyses; given the low prevalence of actionable mutations in the enrolled population and the balanced distribution of known mutation status across arms, this does not materially threaten the primary ORR comparison.

The ITT population is the pre-specified primary analysis population, which is appropriate. The treated population (safety) is nearly identical (98.8% and 98.4% treated), minimizing any ITT vs. per-protocol divergence concern.
Censoring rules for PFS and DoR are standard RECIST-based; no evidence of informative censoring or differential dropout patterns that would bias the secondary endpoints.

deficiencies.description: Margin discrepancy between applicant's pre-specified equivalence margin (0.67, 1.50) and FDA's recommended margin (0.73, 1.36). The study was powered and designed to the wider margin. However, because the observed 90% CI (0.80, 1.09) falls entirely within the stricter FDA margin, this discrepancy has no practical consequence for the approvability determination. This is a non-blocking, documentation-level issue.

final_positions.summary: BLA 761028 for MVASI (bevacizumab-awwb) presents a comprehensive CMC package supporting biosimilarity to US-licensed Avastin. The analytical similarity assessment using 19 bevacizumab-awwb lots, 27 US-licensed Avastin lots, and 29 EU-approved bevacizumab lots is extensive and covers primary structure, higher-order structure, biological activity (Fab- and Fc-mediated), product-related impurities, and process-related impurities. Several attribute differences were identified (high mannose glycans, galactosylation, charge variants, FcγRIIIa 158V binding, aggregates/fragments), but each was adequately characterized and mitigated through orthogonal data, functional assays, and/or clinical PK confirmation. The manufacturing process at Amgen Thousand Oaks (DS) and the designated DP fill site is described as well-controlled and validated. Drug product stability is supported for a 36-month shelf life at 2–8°C. Four post-marketing commitments (PMCs) address residual uncertainties in DS stability acceptance criteria, glycan mapping method validation, HCP detection method validation, and endotoxin detection. None of these residual issues rise to the level of a blocking deficiency; each is appropriately deferred as a PMC. The scientific bridge between bevacizumab-awwb, US-licensed Avastin, and EU-approved bevacizumab is analytically and pharmacokinetically supported. From a CMC perspective, the application meets the standard for approval.
key_concerns: Elevated high mannose glycan content in bevacizumab-awwb relative to US-licensed Avastin and EU-approved bevacizumab, with a noted increasing trend over time in bevacizumab-awwb lots — potential PK impact mitigated by clinical PK data and manufacturing controls, but warrants ongoing monitoring via PMC for glycan mapping method validation.

Differences in charge variant profiles (higher HC C-terminal lysine, differences in acidic and basic peak fractions) — characterized and assessed as clinically inactive based on in vitro potency data and clinical PK; not blocking but requires continued control strategy oversight.
Differences in FcγRIIIa (158V) binding — mitigated by lack of ADCC activity in functional assays and the predominantly soluble VEGFA target MOA; not blocking.

Low endotoxin recovery (LER) issue in the endotoxin detection method — addressed through pyrogen testing at release and a PMC to develop a validated LER-resistant assay; not blocking but must be tracked.
DS stability acceptance criteria for the long-term storage condition require re-evaluation once data from ≥5 lots are available — deferred as PMC; not blocking.

Use of VEGFA111 isoform (not naturally expressed in human tissue or tumors) in the HUVEC proliferation potency assay — acceptability confirmed through orthogonal binding and degradation sensitivity data, but represents a non-standard assay substrate that should be monitored.
HCP detection method validation (including LC-MS and 2D-DIGE) deferred as PMC — not blocking given existing ELISA data and process controls.

deficiencies.description: Elevated and time-trending high mannose glycan content in bevacizumab-awwb lots relative to US-licensed Avastin and EU-approved bevacizumab. Higher high mannose levels can accelerate in vivo clearance via mannose receptor-mediated uptake, potentially affecting PK and efficacy. An increasing trend across bevacizumab-awwb lots was observed. While clinical PK data (Study 20110216 and trough concentrations in Study 20120265) did not demonstrate a PK impact, the glycan mapping method used in the control strategy has not yet been fully validated, and the manufacturing control to cap high mannose content is not yet fully characterized. This is addressable via PMC (glycan mapping method validation and DS stability re-evaluation) and ongoing manufacturing controls, and does not rise to a blocking deficiency given the clinical PK data mitigation.

Low endotoxin recovery (LER) phenomenon identified in the endotoxin detection method used for drug product release. The current approach relies on pyrogen testing as a bridging control at release, which is less specific than a validated LAL method not subject to LER. A PMC has been issued to develop and implement a validated endotoxin detection method not subject to LER. This is a known industry issue with certain formulations and is appropriately managed as a PMC; it does not independently warrant a CRL.

Glycan mapping and HCP detection methods (LC-MS, 2D-DIGE) included in the control strategy have not yet been fully validated at the time of BLA submission. These are deferred as post-marketing commitments. Existing ELISA-based HCP data and the analytical similarity dataset provide adequate assurance for approval, but full method validation is required post-approval to ensure long-term control strategy robustness.
